title: Complexity in number-theoretic sequences arises from their generating rules

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Complexity in number-theoretic sequences arises from their generating rules

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Sequences defined by simple properties of numbers (primes, divisor sums, representations as sums of squares or primes) show complexity that persists despite centuries of number theory, and this complexity arises as a fundamental consequence of the rules generating them, just as in other simple programs.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: such sequences of numbers exhibit complexity that somehow arises as a fundamental consequence of the rules by which the sequences are generated.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 4, “Systems Based on Numbers”; section “The Sequence of Primes” (from p. 132), p. 134. Scope: integer sequences defined by simple number-theoretic properties

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch04-10: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.48

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing databases allow broad empirical comparisons among number-theoretic sequences. They cover selected known objects and cannot isolate the asserted causal interpretation from definition, representation, and research-history effects.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Define complexity metrics and evaluate a preregistered corpus of number-theoretic sequences against matched simple and random baselines, then relate measured complexity to the generating definitions. This can establish complexity for selected sequences but not that their rules are the unique fundamental cause.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Centuries of study is not evidence of intrinsic complexity by itself.

The causal phrase fundamental consequence adds little separable measurable content.

Sequence selection and complexity metrics can bias the result.

fields.value:

data adequacy: 0.42

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The sequences named in the section are public and their proved regularities are catalogued, so the descriptive claim that considerable complexity remains is checkable. The further claim that this complexity arises as a fundamental consequence of the generating rules, in the same sense as in other simple programs, is an interpretation of that remainder. The same tables are compatible with ordinary number-theoretic explanations, so the causal wording is only partly tested.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For primes, divisor sums, sums of squares, and Goldbach-type counts, measure residual complexity after subtracting the regularities number theory has proved. Persistent irregular residuals are compatible with complexity coming from the generating rule; a full short description of each sequence would challenge that reading.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Showing that a sequence looks complex does not show that the complexity is a fundamental consequence of the rule rather than of a specific analytic mechanism.

Several of the sequences are tied to open problems, so 'despite centuries of work' is not itself a complexity measure.
